The variety of declinations is shown by iron needles placed at various latitudes on a <term>terrella</term> <gloss>a small, spherical model of the Earth made of lodestone</gloss>.

<note>A circular diagram represents a terrella, a small magnetic model of the Earth. An outer circle is labeled "Sphere of Virtue" </note><note>original: Orbis Virtutis</note>. Inside, a shaded sphere representing the terrella has a horizontal Axis drawn through it. Along the circumference of this inner sphere, several small iron needles or pins <note>original: obeli</note> are depicted at various latitudes. At the equatorial points at the ends of the axis, the needles lie flat against the surface. As they move toward the top and bottom poles, they incline at increasingly steep angles, until they stand perfectly vertical and perpendicular at the magnetic poles.

The declination of magnetized iron upon a terrella is demonstrated by various equal iron wires, the length of a barleycorn, arranged along a meridian. At the equator, by the power of the stone, the wires are directed toward the poles and lie down upon the body of the stone along the plane of its horizon. The closer they are placed to the poles, the more they are raised up by their rotating nature. At the poles themselves, they reach out perpendicularly toward the very center. However, iron needles do not rise up correctly unless they are on a vigorous stone, or if they are longer than is appropriate.

### CHAPTER III.

### An instrument of demonstration, indicating by the power of the stone the degrees of declination from the horizon of any latitude.

<summary>Gilbert demonstrates how small iron wires or needles tilt at different angles depending on their latitude on a spherical magnet. He introduces a specific instrument designed to measure this magnetic dip or inclination relative to the horizon.</summary>
